items.title: 1.2.1 Square Root of a Complex Number

blocks.text: The square root of a complex number is another complex number that, when squared, gives the original complex number.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This is the same idea as for real numbers: 3 is a square root of 9 because \(3^{2} = 9\). In the same way \(w\) is a square root of \(z\) when \(w^{2} = z\). Every non-zero complex number has exactly two square roots, \(w\) and \(-w\). Below we derive a formula that gives them directly.
Let \(w = p + qi\) be a square root of a complex number \(z = x + iy\), where \(p, q, x, y \in \mathbb{R}\). Then \(w = \sqrt{z}\) ...(i). Taking square on both sides, we get

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the identity true? Expand both sides: \((p^{2}+q^{2})^{2} = p^{4} + 2p^{2}q^{2} + q^{4}\) and \((p^{2}-q^{2})^{2} + 4p^{2}q^{2} = p^{4} - 2p^{2}q^{2} + q^{4} + 4p^{2}q^{2}\), which is the same.
Why only the positive square root in (iv)? \(p\) and \(q\) are real, so \(p^{2} + q^{2}\) can never be negative.

From equations (ii) and (iv), we have \(x = p^{2} - q^{2}\) and \(p^{2} + q^{2} = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\). Adding and subtracting these two equations (the small step the book leaves out):
\[2p^{2} = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} + x\]
\[2q^{2} = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} - x\]
Solving for the values \(p\) and \(q\), we have

q equals plus or minus the square root of (square root of x squared plus y squared, minus x) over 2

items: \(y > 0\), if \(p\) and \(q\) have the same sign

blocks.text: Therefore, the square root of the complex number \(z = x + iy\) is given by

blocks.text_alt: square root of x plus i y equals plus or minus, open bracket, square root of (square root of x squared plus y squared, plus x) over 2, plus i y over modulus of y times square root of (square root of x squared plus y squared, minus x) over 2, close bracket

square root of z equals plus or minus, open bracket, square root of (modulus of z plus x) over 2, plus i y over modulus of y times square root of (modulus of z minus x) over 2, close bracket, equation (v)

blocks.text: Equation (v) is the required formula for the square root of complex numbers.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The factor \(\frac{iy}{|y|}\) is simply \(i\) when \(y > 0\) and \(-i\) when \(y < 0\). So:
if \(y > 0\), the real and imaginary parts of the root have the same sign;
if \(y < 0\), they have opposite signs.
The formula needs \(y \ne 0\). If \(y = 0\), \(z = x\) is real: for \(x > 0\) the roots are \(\pm\sqrt{x}\), for \(x < 0\) they are \(\pm i\sqrt{-x}\).

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem: Find the square root of complex number \(5 + 12i\) and also represent the square roots on an Argand diagram.
steps:
Given: \(z = 5 + 12i\).
To find: both square roots of \(z\), and plot them on an Argand diagram.
Method: use formula (v). It needs \(x\), \(y\) and \(|z|\); the sign of \(y\) tells us whether the two parts of the root have the same sign or opposite signs.

Step 1: Identify \(x\) and \(y\)
\[x + yi = 5 + 12i\]
\[x = 5,\quad y = 12 > 0\]
Why: formula (v) is written in terms of \(x\) and \(y\). Since \(y > 0\), \(\frac{iy}{|y|} = i\): both parts of the root have the same sign.

Step 2: Find the modulus
\[|z| = |5 + 12i| = \sqrt{5^{2} + 12^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169}\]
\[|z| = 13\]
Why: \(|z|\) appears under both square roots in formula (v).

Step 3: Real part of the root
\[\sqrt{\dfrac{|z| + x}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{13+5}{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{9} = 3\]
Why: this is the first square root in formula (v).

Step 4: Imaginary part of the root
\[\dfrac{12i}{|12|}\sqrt{\dfrac{13-5}{2}}\]
\[= i\sqrt{4} = 2i\]
Why: \(\frac{12}{|12|} = 1\), so the factor is just \(i\); then \(\sqrt{(13-5)/2} = \sqrt{4} = 2\).

Step 5: Write the square roots
\[\sqrt{5+12i} = \pm\left(\sqrt{9} + i\sqrt{4}\right)\]
\[= \pm(3 + 2i)\]
Why: the sign \(\pm\) in front gives two square roots, \(3 + 2i\) and \(-3 - 2i\); each is the negative of the other.

Step 6: Represent them on an Argand diagram
\(3 + 2i\) is the point \((3, 2)\) in the first quadrant; \(-3 - 2i\) is the point \((-3, -2)\) in the third quadrant (see the figure below).
Why: on an Argand diagram the real part is measured along the \(x\)-axis and the imaginary part along the \(y\)-axis. The two square roots are always opposite each other through the origin \(O\).
blocks.answer: The square roots of \(5 + 12i\) are \(3 + 2i\) and \(-3 - 2i\), i.e. \(\pm(3 + 2i)\), shown at the points \((3, 2)\) and \((-3, -2)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(w\) is a square root of \(z\) if \(w^{2} = z\); the two square roots are \(w\) and \(-w\).
2. Formula (v): \(\sqrt{z} = \pm\left(\sqrt{\frac{|z|+x}{2}} + \frac{iy}{|y|}\sqrt{\frac{|z|-x}{2}}\right)\).
3. The sign of \(y\) decides the signs: same signs for \(y > 0\), opposite signs for \(y < 0\).
4. On an Argand diagram the two roots lie opposite each other through the origin.
5. Always check by squaring the answer.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing only one root: there are always two, \(\pm\).
2. Ignoring the sign of \(y\): for \(8 - 6i\) the roots are \(\pm(3 - i)\), not \(\pm(3 + i)\).
3. Using \(x^{2} + y^{2}\) instead of \(\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\) inside the formula: \(|z|\) is a square root.
